headline: High: Flowise can write shared server files while OpenHands has broad runtime shell and filesystem control, creating dangerous default-path conflicts and downstream action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write server filesystem and uploaded files, while OpenHands can read/write files in its runtime and use MCP. If Flowise outputs attacker-controlled content into a shared file or mounted path, OpenHands may ingest it as instructions. The bridge is plausible but not proven by the profiles, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Flowise writes untrusted content into a path OpenHands later reads
IF OpenHands parses file contents or MCP-fed content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the two agents onto non-overlapping directories
Disable automatic file ingestion in OpenHands flows
Add a manual review step before OpenHands consumes Flowise outputs
Use read-only mounts for any shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and stores files on the server filesystem; OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and has broad network egress. A shared workspace or mounted volume could expose sensitive chatflow data to OpenHands and then onward through its networked tools. The shared-data pathway is plausible in default deployments, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or mounted volume
IF OpenHands is allowed to transmit file contents through configured tools or model calls
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Restrict OpenHands network egress to approved endpoints
Redact secrets before handing artifacts from Flowise to OpenHands
Rotate any credentials stored in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on the datastore

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Flowise has write_filesystem and shared_state_with_other_instances via server datastore; OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad shell/runtime control. If both target the same directory or repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can clobber each other. The profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces without locking, making high severity justified.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same filesystem path or repository
IF no external lock or lease mechanism serializes their writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes shared state
Disable git mutation in OpenHands for shared repos
Use file locks or a queue for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise is a graph-based agent flow builder that can emit tool-driven outputs, and OpenHands runs an agent loop with shell, browser, and editor actions. If OpenHands treats Flowise output as authoritative, a mistaken or malicious Flowise result can cascade into real actions such as edits or commands. That default-path dependency is dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes Flowise output without verification
IF that output is used to drive shell, browser, or editor actions
mitigations: Require human approval before OpenHands acts on Flowise output
Add schema validation to Flowise outputs
Compare Flowise results against a second source before execution
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis mode for shared tasks
requires-engineering: implement confidence and provenance gates

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, but Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and secrets while OpenHands handles mounted runtime files and model API keys. If regulated data is placed into shared artifacts, differing retention or residency controls could create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction gap, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Flowise chatflows or OpenHands runtime files
IF the deployment applies different retention or deletion policies to those stores
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared artifacts
Document retention settings for both agents
Delete temporary files after each run
Store secrets only in dedicated secret managers
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems
